solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Big shots fail in competitions

indicators.note: one word sitting in another means its letters are placed inside that word

parts.note: cups are trophy competitions, like the FA Cup
to fail in a contest is to lose

explanation.surface: Important people come unstuck in tournaments.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Big shots' looks like VIPs, but it means camera shots taken very near.
explanation.definitionFit: Photographs or film frames taken at very short range make the subject appear large, hence big shots.

clue.text: Visiting church raised father's tone

indicators.note: someone visiting a place is inside it

parts.note: CE is the Church of England

indicators.note: in a down entry, raised means turned upwards, so the word is read bottom to top

parts.note: a sire is a father

explanation.surface: At church, a dad lifts his voice in song.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tone' looks like a musical note in this churchy surface, but it means a shade of colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Cerise is a bright cherry-red colour, and tone is used for a shade or hue.

clue.text: Nightmare of French exam is overwhelming

indicators.note: overwhelming something engulfs it, so one word wraps around the other

parts.note: an oral is a spoken exam
de is French for 'of'

explanation.surface: A French test is a terrible experience for the student.
explanation.walkthrough: ORAL surrounds DE: OR(DE)AL.
explanation.definitionFit: An ordeal is a painful, distressing experience, the waking equivalent of a bad dream.

clue.text: Volatile lover of old guy keeps it hidden

parts.note: an ex is a former partner

indicators.note: something that keeps another thing holds it inside

parts.note: a guy is a rope or cable bracing a tent or mast
taken as written

explanation.surface: A temperamental former partner of some man is concealing something.
explanation.walkthrough: EX, then CABLE holding IT: C(IT)ABLE.
explanation.definitionFit: Volatile people are liable to sudden outbursts of emotion, being easily stirred up and quick-tempered.

clue.text: Sticking up for public transport, issue a tirade

parts.note: pro means in favour of
the Tube is the London Underground
to rant is to deliver a tirade

explanation.surface: Defending the Underground, someone launches into a furious speech.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sticking up for' reads as defending, but the definition stops at 'up'.
explanation.definitionFit: Protuberant means bulging or projecting outward from a surface, like something jutting upward.

clue.text: Update backing state politician

indicators.note: backing means going backwards, so the word for state is read from its end

parts.note: to aver is to state firmly
MP is a Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: Revising the policy that supports a nation's leader.
explanation.walkthrough: AVER reversed is REVA, then MP is added.
explanation.definitionFit: To revamp something is to renovate or modernise it, giving it a fresh version.

clue.text: A Green revolutionary's gripping message

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the colour word is read backwards
gripping something holds it tightly within

parts.note: lime is a shade of green
taken as written

explanation.surface: An environmental activist sends a gripping communiqué.
explanation.walkthrough: LIME reversed is EMIL, which grips A: EM(A)IL.
explanation.definitionFit: An email is an electronic communication sent over the internet, a kind of note or letter.

clue.text: Cocktail of pear vermouth provided as this?

definitions.text: Cocktail of pear vermouth provided as this?

indicators.note: a cocktail is a mixture, so the letters of the fruit are shaken up

parts.note: taken as written
it is short for Italian vermouth, as in gin and it
if means provided that

explanation.surface: A pear and vermouth mix might be served before dinner.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue also describes the answer: such a mixed drink could be served as one. Gin and it is a British name for gin with Italian vermouth.
explanation.definitionFit: An aperitif is an alcoholic drink taken before a meal to stimulate the appetite.

clue.text: Pray, keeping high hopes, ignoring a forecast

indicators.note: keeping something means holding it inside
ignoring something leaves it out, so the letter named next is dropped

parts.note: taken as written
the letter removed

indicators.note: high can mean intoxicated, so the next word's letters are in disorder

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone prays with great optimism rather than predicting coldly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'High hopes' reads as one phrase, but 'high' is the signal to jumble the word after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To prophesy is to predict what will happen, a verb for foretelling future events.

clue.text: Editor's study vacated by a cast member

indicators.note: a place vacated by someone has lost that occupant, so the letter named next leaves the word

parts.note: to study a subject at university is to read it
the letter that leaves
a member of a play's cast is an actor

explanation.surface: An editor's office has been emptied by someone from the play.
explanation.walkthrough: READ loses its A to become RED, then ACTOR follows. The 's stands for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: A redactor prepares text for publication, revising or censoring it, which is the work of someone who edits.

clue.text: Lad taken short behind peer's summerhouse

indicators.note: something taken short is cut down, so the word for lad loses its final letter

parts.note: to peer is to look intently, to gaze
a lad is a boy

explanation.surface: A boy caught needing the loo behind a lord's garden house.
explanation.walkthrough: BOY minus its last letter is BO, placed behind GAZE. 'Taken short' is a British idiom for suddenly needing a toilet; a peer is also a lord.
explanation.definitionFit: A gazebo is a small open garden pavilion, the kind of summerhouse giving a view of grounds.

clue.text: Insufficient time to finish examination

parts.note: a scan is a medical examination
T for time, placed at the finish

explanation.surface: Not enough time is left to complete the test.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Time to finish' tells you T goes at the end, after SCAN.
explanation.definitionFit: Scant means barely sufficient or meagre, describing a quantity that falls short of what is needed.

clue.text: Kind of advice ignoring the company angle

indicators.note: ignoring something leaves it out, so the abbreviation for company is dropped from the word for advice

parts.note: counsel is advice
CO is the abbreviation for company, the part removed
to angle is to fish with rod and line

explanation.surface: Some type of guidance that disregards the firm's point of view.
explanation.walkthrough: COUNSEL without CO is UNSEL, then FISH. 'Kind of' looks like it means 'type of', but 'Kind' alone is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone kind puts others first and thinks generously, the essence of being free of selfishness.

clue.text: Contributions from U-boat patrols?

parts.note: a U-boat is a German submarine
patrols are military missions

explanation.surface: Wartime submarine sorties supply entries.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'U-boat patrols' is a whimsical split of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Submissions are pieces of work handed in or offered, such as entries sent to a magazine.

clue.text: Pint pots?

parts.note: surface reading: drinking vessels that hold a pint
setter's reading: pot bellies produced by many pints

explanation.walkthrough: A pot is also a round paunch, so a 'pint pot' is a stomach built from pints of ale.
explanation.definitionFit: Paunches developed by heavy drinking are the potbellies that pints of ale build over years.

clue.text: Come down south to head Panorama

parts.note: an aircraft comes down to land
S is the abbreviation for south
a head or headland is a cape

explanation.surface: Descend southward to present a BBC current affairs programme.
explanation.walkthrough: Panorama is a long-running BBC current affairs show, which the capital letter hints at.
explanation.definitionFit: A landscape is a wide view of scenery, and a panorama is just such a sweeping vista.

clue.text: Fit mock rings? He might do

definitions.text: Fit mock rings? He might do

indicators.note: to ring something is to encircle it, so one word surrounds the other

parts.note: to mock is to jeer
fit means healthy, well

explanation.surface: Could someone fit imitation rings? A craftsman might.
explanation.walkthrough: JEER rings WELL: JE(WELL)ER. Read whole, the clue describes the tradesman who fits and sells rings, including fakes.
explanation.definitionFit: A jeweller makes, sizes and repairs rings and other ornaments, so fitting rings is the trade.

clue.text: Painter's spirit tipped over a table

indicators.note: tipped over in a down entry means upended, so the word is read upwards

parts.note: rum is a spirit
taken as written
a table of figures is a list

explanation.surface: An artist's drink got knocked onto a piece of furniture.
explanation.walkthrough: RUM reversed is MUR, then A and LIST.
explanation.definitionFit: A muralist creates large pictures on walls, so is an artist who works in paint.

clue.text: Count and mountaineer scrambled together

indicators.note: scrambled describes things jumbled up, so these letters are mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A nobleman and a climber clamber up a rock face side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: An enumeration is a numbering or listing of items one by one, the act of making a tally.

clue.text: A game even love comes into

indicators.note: a letter coming into a word enters it, sitting inside

parts.note: being quits means being even, owing nothing
love is zero in tennis, shaped like O

explanation.surface: A match finishes level, with a nil score figuring in it.
explanation.walkthrough: Being 'quits' is an informal way of saying two people are even, with nothing owed.
explanation.definitionFit: Quoits is a pastime of throwing rings at a peg, an old pub and deck sport.

clue.text: How some feathers were used in trees

parts.note: as can mean how, as in 'do as you like'
quill feathers were once cut and used for writing

explanation.surface: A puzzle about how birds' plumage was employed among the branches.
explanation.walkthrough: Before steel nibs, goose quills were cut to a point and dipped in ink for writing.
explanation.definitionFit: Aspens are poplar species with fluttering leaves, a common kind of deciduous tree.

clue.text: Wastes spies infiltrating European partners

parts.note: E is the abbreviation for European

indicators.note: agents infiltrating a group get inside it, so these letters go within the others

parts.note: mates are partners
the CIA is the American spy agency

explanation.surface: Secret agents get in among a group of colleagues from the Continent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wastes' is a verb here, meaning makes thin, not a noun for barren land.
explanation.definitionFit: To emaciate is to make thin and weak, so the verb means wears away the body's flesh.

clue.text: Creature caged in that is furious

indicators.note: an animal caged in something is enclosed by it

parts.note: i.e. is short for id est, Latin for 'that is'
a rat is a creature

explanation.surface: An animal locked up is understandably angry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'That is' looks like part of the sentence, but it is the phrase abbreviated i.e.
explanation.definitionFit: Irate describes someone very angry, livid or seething with temper.

clue.text: Help to protect country markets

indicators.note: to protect something is to surround it, so the letters for country are held inside

parts.note: SOS is a distress call for help
UK, the United Kingdom

explanation.surface: Aid to safeguard rural trading fairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A souk is an open-air marketplace in Arab countries, a bazaar of stalls.

clue.text: Secular figures in formulaic altarpieces

indicators.note: the answer figures in, or appears within, the next words, running across them

parts.note: letters running across the two words

explanation.surface: Non-religious figures appear in some predictable church paintings.
explanation.definitionFit: Laical relates to the laity, people outside the clergy, so it means not of the church.

clue.text: Papers found by a fellow in Ilium, possibly authentic

indicators.note: these pieces placed in a word sit inside it

parts.note: the ilium is a hip bone; 'possibly' marks it as an example
taken as written
F is the abbreviation for fellow
identity papers, ID

explanation.surface: Documents discovered by a scholar in ancient Troy may be genuine.
explanation.walkthrough: Ilium is also the Latin name of Troy, the surface's setting; 'possibly' marks the hip bone as just one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Bona fide is Latin for 'in good faith' and is used to mean genuine, real and not fake.

clue.text: Evil is clear to men in retrospect

indicators.note: retrospect looks back, so the letters are read from the end

parts.note: nett means clear, as in profit after deductions
OR is other ranks, ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: Looking back, wickedness is obvious to the troops.
explanation.walkthrough: NETT plus OR reversed gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rotten can describe something morally corrupt or wicked, as in a rotten scoundrel.

clue.text: Slanders by fools are spread around

indicators.note: something spread around another thing encloses it

parts.note: asses are fools
per means by, as in 'per post'

explanation.surface: Malicious gossip from idiots gets passed about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spread around' suggests rumours circulating, but it tells one word to enclose another.
explanation.definitionFit: To asperse is to attack someone's reputation with damaging claims, the same as defaming them.
